notes.front: What is memory protection, as SP 800-53 control SI-16 frames it?
notes.back: Controls that protect system memory from unauthorised code execution.
notes.explanation: SI-16 leaves the exact controls for each organisation to assign; the aim is that memory cannot be used to run code that should not run.
notes.example: Like marking some rooms of a building "storage only": things may be kept there, but nobody may start work in them.
notes.evidence: Implement the following controls to protect the system memory from unauthorized code execution: [Assignment: organization-defined controls].
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SI-16 Memory Protection, PDF p. 382

notes.front: What is process isolation, as SP 800-53 control SC-39 frames it?
notes.back: Maintaining a separate execution domain for each executing system process.
notes.explanation: SC-39 notes that a system can do this by giving each process a separate address space.
notes.example: Like separate hotel rooms: each guest has their own space, and one guest cannot rearrange another's room.
notes.evidence: Maintain a separate execution domain for each executing system process. Discussion: Systems can maintain separate execution domains for each executing process by assigning each process a separate address space.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-39 Process Isolation, PDF p. 351

notes.front: What is a cryptographic module, as SP 800-175B defines it?
notes.back: The hardware, software and/or firmware that implements approved security functions and is contained within a cryptographic boundary.
notes.explanation: SP 800-175B names cryptographic algorithms and key generation among those approved security functions.
notes.example: Like a bank vault with its own walls: all the sensitive work happens inside one clearly drawn boundary.
notes.evidence: approved security functions (including cryptographic algorithms and key generation) and is contained within a cryptographic boundary
notes.source: NIST SP 800-175B Rev. 1, Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards in the Federal Government: Cryptographic Mechanisms, Section 1.5 Glossary, PDF p. 13

notes.front: What is a trusted platform module (TPM)?
notes.back: A cryptographic module that can establish device identity, securely store keys and credentials, and measure and report system state.
notes.explanation: SP 800-175B lists these "among other capabilities", so the list is not exhaustive.
notes.example: Like a small safe built into a laptop's motherboard that also keeps a record of how the laptop started up.
notes.evidence: A TPM is a cryptographic module that can, among other capabilities, establish device identity in a platform, provide secure storage for keys and credentials, and support the measurement and reporting of the system state.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-175B Rev. 1, Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards in the Federal Government: Cryptographic Mechanisms, Section 2.3, Trusted Computing Group, PDF p. 28

notes.front: In multilevel security, what is aggregation?
notes.back: Assembling and combining information of a lower security class, which can reveal information of a higher class.
notes.explanation: NISTIR 7316 describes this as a covert channel through which information can pass even under mandatory access control.
notes.example: Like collecting individually harmless jigsaw pieces from several boxes until the whole picture appears.
notes.evidence: However, information can pass through a covert channel in MAC, where information of a higher security class is deduced by inference such as assembling and intelligently combining information of a lower security class.
notes.source: NISTIR 7316, Assessment of Access Control Systems, Section 2.2.2.1 Mandatory access control, PDF p. 16

notes.front: In multilevel security, what is inference?
notes.back: Deducing information of a higher security class from information of a lower security class.
notes.explanation: NISTIR 7316 gives assembling and intelligently combining lower-class information as one way it happens.
notes.example: Like working out that a colleague is leaving because their desk is being emptied and their leaving card is going round.
notes.evidence: information of a higher security class is deduced by inference such as assembling and intelligently combining information of a lower security class
notes.source: NISTIR 7316, Assessment of Access Control Systems, Section 2.2.2.1 Mandatory access control, PDF p. 16

notes.front: What is operational technology (OT)?
notes.back: Programmable systems and devices that interact with the physical environment, or manage devices that do.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82r3 says these systems detect or cause a direct change by monitoring or controlling devices, processes and events.
notes.example: Like the office network, but wired to valves, motors and doors rather than only to screens.
notes.evidence: OT encompasses a broad range of programmable systems and devices that interact with the physical environment (or manage devices that interact with the physical environment). These systems and devices detect or cause a direct change through the monitoring and/or control of devices, processes, and events.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Executive Summary, PDF p. 18

notes.front: What is an industrial control system (ICS)?
notes.back: Control components (such as electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic) acting together to achieve an industrial objective, such as manufacturing.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82r3 also lists transporting matter or energy as an industrial objective.
notes.example: Like a bottling line: sensors, motors and controllers working together so that every bottle is filled and capped.
notes.evidence: An ICS consists of combinations of control components (e.g., electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic) that act together to achieve an industrial objective (e.g., manufacturing, transportation of matter or energy).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Glossary, PDF p. 180

notes.front: What is supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)?
notes.back: A computerised system that gathers and processes data and applies operational controls over long distances.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82r3 gives power transmission and distribution, and pipeline systems, as typical uses.
notes.example: Like an air-traffic control room, but watching pumps and valves spread across a whole region.
notes.evidence: A generic name for a computerized system that is capable of gathering and processing data and applying operational controls over long distances. Typical uses include power transmission and distribution and pipeline systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Glossary, PDF p. 184

notes.front: What is a programmable logic controller (PLC)?
notes.back: A solid-state control system with user-programmable memory that stores instructions for functions such as I/O control, logic and timing.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82r3 also lists counting, communication, arithmetic and data processing among the functions.
notes.example: Like a rugged little computer bolted into a factory cabinet, running one control program all day.
notes.evidence: A solid-state control system that has a user-programmable memory for storing instructions for the purpose of implementing specific functions such as I/O control, logic, timing, counting, three mode (PID) control, communication, arithmetic, and data and file processing.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Glossary, PDF p. 182

notes.front: What is cloud computing, as SP 800-145 defines it?
notes.back: A model for on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources, rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 gives networks, servers, storage, applications and services as examples of the resources.
notes.example: Like the electricity grid: you draw what you need from a shared supply instead of running your own generator.
notes.evidence: Cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (e.g., networks, servers, storage, applications, and services) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is Software as a Service (SaaS)?
notes.back: The consumer uses the provider's applications running on a cloud infrastructure.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 says the applications are reached from client devices through a thin client, such as a web browser, or a program interface.
notes.example: Like renting a furnished flat: you live in it, and the landlord looks after the building and the furniture.
notes.evidence: The capability provided to the consumer is to use the provider’s applications running on a cloud infrastructure 2. The applications are accessible from various client devices through either a thin client interface, such as a web browser (e.g., web-based email), or a program interface.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Service Models, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is Platform as a Service (PaaS)?
notes.back: The consumer deploys applications it created or acquired onto the provider's cloud infrastructure.
notes.explanation: The applications are the consumer's own or acquired ones, which is what separates PaaS from SaaS, where the consumer uses the provider's applications.
notes.example: Like renting a fitted commercial kitchen: you bring your own recipes and ingredients, and the owner maintains the ovens.
notes.evidence: The capability provided to the consumer is to deploy onto the cloud infrastructure consumer-created or acquired applications
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Service Models, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
notes.back: The consumer provisions processing, storage, networks and other fundamental resources, and can deploy and run arbitrary software, including operating systems.
notes.explanation: Unlike SaaS and PaaS consumers, the IaaS consumer can run operating systems as well as applications.
notes.example: Like renting an empty warehouse: the landlord keeps the building standing; you install and run everything inside.
notes.evidence: The capability provided to the consumer is to provision processing, storage, networks, and other fundamental computing resources where the consumer is able to deploy and run arbitrary software, which can include operating systems and applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Service Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: What is the Internet of Things (IoT), and what makes something an IoT device?
notes.back: Internet-ready products; an IoT device has at least one transducer (sensor or actuator) and at least one network interface.
notes.explanation: In NIST IR 8259r1 the transducer interacts with the physical world and the network interface with the digital world.
notes.example: Like a smart smoke alarm: it senses smoke and sends an alert to a phone over Wi-Fi.
notes.evidence: An IoT device has at least one transducer (sensor or actuator) for interacting directly with the physical world and at least one network interface (e.g., Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Long-Term Evolution (LTE), Zigbee, Ultra-Wideband (UWB)) for interfacing with the digital world.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Section 1, Introduction, PDF p. 9

notes.front: What is a microservice, in SP 800-204?
notes.back: A small component of an application, typically implementing a single business function, that talks to other components over lightweight protocols.
notes.explanation: SP 800-204 lists development agility from these small, less complex codebases among the incentives for the design.
notes.example: Like a food court instead of one big restaurant: each stall makes one dish and passes orders to the others.
notes.evidence: components called microservices that communicate with each other using lightweight communication protocols. Incentives to design and deploy a microservices-based application system include: (a) agility in development due to relatively small and less complex codebases since each one typically implements a single business function
notes.source: NIST SP 800-204, Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is an API gateway in a microservices application?
notes.back: A single entry point through which all clients reach the application's many component microservices.
notes.explanation: SP 800-204 motivates it by noting that a microservices application consists of many fine-grained endpoints.
notes.example: Like a hotel reception desk: guests ask in one place, and staff route each request to the right department.
notes.evidence: consists of multiple fine-grained endpoints. Hence, it makes sense to provide a single entry point for all clients to multiple component microservices of the application.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-204, Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems, Section 2.3, API Gateway, PDF p. 17

notes.front: What is containerisation?
notes.back: Packaging and running applications in containers: operating system virtualisation combined with application software packaging.
notes.explanation: SP 800-190 describes containers as a portable, reusable and automatable way to package and run applications.
notes.example: Like shipping containers: the same sealed box moves between ship, train and lorry without being repacked.
notes.evidence: Application container technologies, also known as containers, are a form of operating system virtualization combined with application software packaging. Containers provide a portable, reusable, and automatable way to package and run applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Abstract, PDF p. 4

notes.front: What is serverless computing?
notes.back: Computing that hides servers from the user: the provider runs the machines and provisioning, scales resources with demand automatically, and charges per use.
notes.explanation: Tasks such as operating system maintenance, security updates and capacity planning pass to the provider, which isolates users sharing a physical machine through virtualisation. The term spans services from Platform as a Service to Software as a Service.
notes.example: Uploading code that the provider runs only when it is needed, and paying for that use alone rather than for idle servers.
notes.evidence: Serverless Computing abstracts servers away from the user. Operational management falls to the service provider, including handling physical machines and VM provisioning.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Serverless”

notes.front: What is edge computing, as SP 800-82r3 describes it?
notes.back: A decentralised infrastructure where computing resources and application services are distributed along the path between the data source and the cloud.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82r3 says it runs vertically from device to cloud and horizontally across industrial IoT subsystems.
notes.example: Like a local branch office that handles routine work so that not everything travels to head office.
notes.evidence: Edge computing is a decentralized computing infrastructure in which computing resources and application services can be distributed along the communication path between the data source and the cloud. It exists vertically within the full stack (i.e., from the device to the cloud) and horizontally across IIoT subsystems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Section 2.3.8, Industrial Internet of Things, PDF p. 44

notes.front: What is a hypervisor?
notes.back: Software that manages guest operating systems on a host and controls the flow of instructions between them and the physical hardware.
notes.explanation: SP 800-125 names the processor, disk storage, memory and network interface cards as the hardware it mediates.
notes.example: Like a building manager sharing one building's power, water and rooms among several tenants.
notes.evidence: The guest OSs on a host are managed by the hypervisor. which controls the flow of instructions between the guest OSs and the physical hardware, such as CPU, disk storage, memory, and network interface cards.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is a type 1 hypervisor?
notes.back: A bare-metal (native) hypervisor: it runs directly on the hardware, with no host operating system underneath.
notes.explanation: SP 800-125 calls it bare-metal virtualisation rather than type 1, and adds that such a hypervisor can even be built into the computer's firmware.
notes.example: Like a landlord who owns the land itself, rather than subletting rooms inside someone else's house.
notes.evidence: In bare metal virtualization, also known as native virtualization, the hypervisor runs directly on the underlying hardware, without a host OS; the hypervisor can even be built into the computer’s firmware.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies, Section 2, Full Virtualization Overview, PDF p. 11

notes.front: SP 800-53 SI-16 names {{c1::data execution prevention}} and address space layout randomisation among the controls that protect memory.
notes.explanation: The discussion ties these controls to adversaries who try to run code in non-executable or prohibited memory.
notes.evidence: Some adversaries launch attacks with the intent of executing code in non-executable regions of memory or in memory locations that are prohibited. Controls employed to protect memory include data execution prevention and address space layout randomization.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SI-16 Memory Protection, PDF p. 382

notes.front: An attacker overflows a buffer in a server program and tries to run the injected code from a region of memory marked non-executable. Which capability is designed to stop this?
notes.back: Memory protection.
notes.choices:
A) Memory protection
B) Process isolation
C) Trusted platform module
notes.choicesExplained: B: process isolation keeps processes in separate execution domains; it is not aimed at code run from non-executable memory. C: a TPM stores keys and measures system state.
notes.explanation: SI-16 is aimed at adversaries who try to execute code in non-executable or prohibited regions of memory.
notes.evidence: Some adversaries launch attacks with the intent of executing code in non-executable regions of memory or in memory locations that are prohibited.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SI-16 Memory Protection, PDF p. 382

notes.front: SP 800-53 SC-39 names {{c1::sandboxing}} and virtualisation among process isolation technologies.
notes.explanation: Such technologies logically separate software and firmware, limiting what potentially untrusted software can reach.
notes.evidence: Process isolation technologies, including sandboxing or virtualization, logically separate software and firmware from other software, firmware, and data. Process isolation helps limit the access of potentially untrusted software to other system resources.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-39 Process Isolation, PDF p. 351

notes.front: Under SC-39 enhancement (1), why is hardware separation of processes preferred to software separation?
notes.back: It is generally less susceptible to compromise, so it gives greater assurance that the separation will be enforced.
notes.explanation: Keep the hedge: SP 800-53 says "generally", not always.
notes.evidence: Hardware-based separation of system processes is generally less susceptible to compromise than software-based separation, thus providing greater assurance that the separation will be enforced.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-39(1) Hardware Separation, PDF p. 351

notes.front: A browser runs each tab in its own sandboxed process with its own address space, so a malicious page cannot alter code running in another tab. Which capability is this?
notes.back: Process isolation.
notes.choices:
A) Process isolation
B) Memory protection
C) Aggregation
notes.choicesExplained: B: memory protection targets unauthorised code execution in memory, not keeping processes apart. C: aggregation is combining lower-class information, not a system capability.
notes.explanation: With a distinct address space per process, one process cannot modify the executing code of another.
notes.evidence: Each system process has a distinct address space so that communication between processes is performed in a manner controlled through the security functions, and one process cannot modify the executing code of another process.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-39 Process Isolation, PDF p. 351

notes.front: A firm wants each laptop to keep its disk-encryption keys in dedicated hardware on the motherboard, which can also report whether the start-up state has changed. Which component fits?
notes.back: A trusted platform module (TPM).
notes.choices:
A) A trusted platform module (TPM)
B) An API gateway
C) A hypervisor
notes.choicesExplained: B: an API gateway is the entry point to microservices. C: a hypervisor manages guest operating systems; it is not a key store.
notes.explanation: SP 800-175B says a TPM can provide secure storage for keys and support measuring and reporting the system state.
notes.evidence: A TPM is a cryptographic module that can, among other capabilities, establish device identity in a platform, provide secure storage for keys and credentials, and support the measurement and reporting of the system state.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-175B Rev. 1, Guideline for Using Cryptographic Standards in the Federal Government: Cryptographic Mechanisms, Section 2.3, Trusted Computing Group, PDF p. 28

notes.front: FIPS 140-3 provides {{c1::four}} increasing, qualitative levels of security for cryptographic modules.
notes.explanation: The levels are meant to cover a wide range of potential applications and environments.
notes.evidence: The standard provides four increasing, qualitative levels of security intended to cover a wide range of potential applications and environments.
notes.source: FIPS 140-3, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, Abstract, PDF p. 3

notes.front: Under FIPS 140-3, what follows when a cryptographic module is validated under the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP)?
notes.back: The module is considered to conform to FIPS 140-3.
notes.explanation: FIPS 140-3 points to CMVP validation as the route by which modules are treated as conforming.
notes.evidence: Cryptographic modules that are validated under the CMVP will be considered as conforming to this standard.
notes.source: FIPS 140-3, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, Section 9, Implementations, PDF p. 5

notes.front: A US federal agency is buying an encrypting storage product and needs its cryptographic module to count as conforming to FIPS 140-3. What should it check?
notes.back: That the module is validated under the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP).
notes.choices:
A) That the module is validated under the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP)
B) That the product runs on a hosted hypervisor
C) That the product sits behind an API gateway
notes.choicesExplained: B: the hypervisor type says nothing about conformance of the cryptography. C: an API gateway is an entry point to microservices, not a validation.
notes.explanation: FIPS 140-3 says modules validated under the CMVP will be considered as conforming to the standard.
notes.evidence: Cryptographic modules that are validated under the CMVP will be considered as conforming to this standard.
notes.source: FIPS 140-3, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, Section 9, Implementations, PDF p. 5

notes.front: What are two areas that FIPS 140-3's security requirements cover?
notes.back: Any two, for example physical security, self-tests, sensitive security parameter management.
notes.explanation: The requirements span the secure design, implementation and operation of a cryptographic module.
notes.evidence: The security requirements cover areas related to the secure design, implementation and operation of a cryptographic module. These areas include cryptographic module specification; cryptographic module interfaces; roles, services, and authentication; software/firmware security; operating environment; physical security; non-invasive security; sensitive security parameter management; self-tests; life-cycle assurance; and mitigation of other attacks.
notes.source: FIPS 140-3, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, Abstract, PDF p. 3

notes.front: An analyst cleared to Secret collects several Unclassified supply reports and, by combining them, works out the date of a Top Secret operation. What has happened?
notes.back: Inference through aggregation of lower-class information.
notes.choices:
A) Inference through aggregation of lower-class information
B) A write-down to a lower label
C) A failure of process isolation
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing was written to a lower label; the analyst only read and combined. C: process isolation concerns separate execution domains for processes, not what people deduce.
notes.explanation: NISTIR 7316 notes that higher-class information can be deduced by assembling and combining lower-class information, a covert channel that can pass even under mandatory access control.
notes.evidence: However, information can pass through a covert channel in MAC, where information of a higher security class is deduced by inference such as assembling and intelligently combining information of a lower security class.
notes.source: NISTIR 7316, Assessment of Access Control Systems, Section 2.2.2.1 Mandatory access control, PDF p. 16

notes.front: Aggregation versus inference: which is the act of combining lower-class information, and which is the deduction it allows?
notes.back: Aggregation is the assembling and combining; inference is deducing the higher-class information from it.
notes.explanation: NISTIR 7316 names assembling and combining as one way inference happens, so aggregation can feed inference.
notes.evidence: information of a higher security class is deduced by inference such as assembling and intelligently combining information of a lower security class
notes.source: NISTIR 7316, Assessment of Access Control Systems, Section 2.2.2.1 Mandatory access control, PDF p. 16

notes.front: Besides industrial control systems, what are two kinds of system SP 800-82r3 gives as examples of OT?
notes.back: Any two, for example building automation, transportation or physical access control systems.
notes.explanation: Each of them monitors or controls devices, processes and events in the physical world.
notes.evidence: These systems and devices detect or cause a direct change through the monitoring and/or control of devices, processes, and events. Examples include industrial control systems (ICS), building automation systems, transportation systems, physical access control systems, physical environment monitoring systems, and physical environment measurement systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Executive Summary, PDF p. 18

notes.front: According to SP 800-82r3, what do OT systems tend to prioritise over other factors such as confidentiality?
notes.back: Availability and safety.
notes.explanation: Keep the hedge: SP 800-82r3 says OT systems "tend to" do this, because they operate under different environments and requirements from information technology systems.
notes.evidence: OT systems operate under different environments and requirements than IT systems. For example, OT systems tend to prioritize availability and safety over other factors like confidentiality.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Section 4.1.1, Building the business case, PDF p. 53

notes.front: What are two kinds of risk that SP 800-82r3 says set OT apart from traditional information technology?
notes.back: Any two: risk to human health and safety, serious damage to the environment, financial issues such as lost production.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82r3 presents these as part of OT's different risks and priorities.
notes.evidence: OT has many characteristics that differ from traditional IT systems, including different risks and priorities. Some of these include significant risk to the health and safety of human lives, serious damage to the environment, and financial issues, such as production losses.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Section 3, Comparing OT and IT System Security, PDF p. 45

notes.front: A water utility must decide how to patch the controllers at a treatment plant that has to run around the clock. Which concerns does SP 800-82r3 say OT tends to put first?
notes.back: Availability and safety.
notes.choices:
A) Availability and safety
B) Confidentiality above all
C) Non-repudiation of operator actions
notes.choicesExplained: B: SP 800-82r3 says OT tends to rank confidentiality below availability and safety. C: non-repudiation is not named as an OT priority.
notes.explanation: OT systems tend to prioritise availability and safety over other factors like confidentiality, so a patch plan must avoid stopping the plant or making it unsafe.
notes.evidence: For example, OT systems tend to prioritize availability and safety over other factors like confidentiality.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Section 4.1.1, Building the business case, PDF p. 53

notes.front: SCADA systems control {{c1::dispersed}} assets for which centralised data acquisition is as important as control.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82r3 names water distribution, oil and gas pipelines, electrical grids and rail among such distribution systems.
notes.evidence: Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems are used to control dispersed assets for which centralized data acquisition is as important as control [Bailey][Boyer]. These systems are used in distribution systems, such as water distribution and wastewater collection systems, oil and natural gas pipelines, electrical utility transmission and distribution systems, and rail and other public transportation systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Section 2.3.2, SCADA Systems, PDF p. 29

notes.front: A gas company monitors pressure and opens or closes valves along a 600 km pipeline from one control centre. Which kind of system is this most typically?
notes.back: SCADA.
notes.choices:
A) SCADA
B) A single programmable logic controller
C) Platform as a Service
notes.choicesExplained: B: a PLC is a local control component, not a system for gathering data and controlling assets over long distances. C: PaaS is a cloud service model for deploying applications.
notes.explanation: SCADA gathers data and applies operational controls over long distances, and pipeline systems are a typical use.
notes.evidence: A generic name for a computerized system that is capable of gathering and processing data and applying operational controls over long distances. Typical uses include power transmission and distribution and pipeline systems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Glossary, PDF p. 184

notes.front: Which essential cloud characteristic lets a consumer provision capabilities automatically, without human interaction with each service provider?
notes.back: On-demand self-service.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 gives server time and network storage as examples of what can be provisioned this way.
notes.evidence: On-demand self-service. A consumer can unilaterally provision computing capabilities, such as server time and network storage, as needed automatically without requiring human interaction with each service provider.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Essential Characteristics, PDF p. 6

notes.front: Which essential cloud characteristic means capabilities are reached over the network through standard mechanisms from varied thin or thick clients?
notes.back: Broad network access.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 names mobile phones, tablets, laptops and workstations as such client platforms.
notes.evidence: Broad network access. Capabilities are available over the network and accessed through standard mechanisms that promote use by heterogeneous thin or thick client platforms (e.g., mobile phones, tablets, laptops, and workstations).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Essential Characteristics, PDF p. 6

notes.front: Which essential cloud characteristic pools the provider's resources to serve many consumers using a multi-tenant model?
notes.back: Resource pooling.
notes.explanation: Physical and virtual resources are dynamically assigned and reassigned according to consumer demand.
notes.evidence: Resource pooling. The provider’s computing resources are pooled to serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model, with different physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned and reassigned according to consumer demand.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Essential Characteristics, PDF p. 6

notes.front: Which essential cloud characteristic lets capabilities be provisioned and released, sometimes automatically, to scale outward and inward with demand?
notes.back: Rapid elasticity.
notes.explanation: To the consumer, the capabilities available often appear unlimited.
notes.evidence: Rapid elasticity. Capabilities can be elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand. To the consumer, the capabilities available for provisioning often appear to be unlimited
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Essential Characteristics, PDF p. 6

notes.front: Which essential cloud characteristic meters resource use so that it can be monitored, controlled and reported?
notes.back: Measured service.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 says this gives transparency to both the provider and the consumer.
notes.evidence: Resource usage can be monitored, controlled, and reported, providing transparency for both the provider and consumer of the utilized service.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Essential Characteristics, PDF p. 6

notes.front: During a sales peak a retailer's cloud capacity grows automatically, then shrinks again when the peak ends. Which essential characteristic is this?
notes.back: Rapid elasticity.
notes.choices:
A) Rapid elasticity
B) Broad network access
C) Measured service
notes.choicesExplained: B: broad network access is about reaching capabilities over the network from varied clients. C: measured service is about metering and reporting use, not scaling it.
notes.explanation: Rapid elasticity means scaling outward and inward commensurate with demand, in some cases automatically.
notes.evidence: Capabilities can be elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Essential Characteristics, PDF p. 6

notes.front: SaaS versus IaaS: who controls the operating systems?
notes.back: SaaS: the provider; the consumer controls none of the infrastructure. IaaS: the consumer controls operating systems, storage and deployed applications.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 gives the SaaS consumer at most limited user-specific application settings, while the IaaS consumer runs arbitrary software.
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure but has control over operating systems, storage, and deployed applications; and possibly limited control of select networking components (e.g., host firewalls).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Service Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: A start-up rents virtual servers from a provider, installs its own operating system and runs its own database on them. Which service model is this?
notes.back: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).
notes.choices:
A) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
B) Platform as a Service (PaaS)
C) Software as a Service (SaaS)
notes.choicesExplained: B: in PaaS the consumer does not control the operating systems. C: in SaaS the consumer only uses the provider's applications.
notes.explanation: Only in IaaS does the consumer control operating systems as well as storage and deployed applications.
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure but has control over operating systems, storage, and deployed applications
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Service Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: Developers push their own code to a provider's platform in a language the provider supports; they never manage servers, operating systems or storage. Which service model is this?
notes.back: Platform as a Service (PaaS).
notes.choices:
A) Platform as a Service (PaaS)
B) Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
C) Software as a Service (SaaS)
notes.choicesExplained: B: in IaaS the consumer would control the operating systems. C: in SaaS the consumer uses the provider's applications, not its own code.
notes.explanation: In PaaS the consumer controls the deployed applications but not the underlying network, servers, operating systems or storage.
notes.evidence: The consumer does not manage or control the underlying cloud infrastructure including network, servers, operating systems, or storage, but has control over the deployed applications and possibly configuration settings for the application-hosting environment.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Service Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: Which cloud deployment model is provisioned for exclusive use by a single organisation comprising multiple consumers?
notes.back: Private cloud.
notes.explanation: It may be run by the organisation, a third party or both, and may exist on or off premises.
notes.evidence: Private cloud. The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization comprising multiple consumers (e.g., business units). It may be owned, managed, and operated by the organization, a third party, or some combination of them, and it may exist on or off premises.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: Which cloud deployment model is provisioned for exclusive use by consumers from organisations that have shared concerns?
notes.back: Community cloud.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 lists mission, security requirements, policy and compliance considerations as examples of shared concerns.
notes.evidence: Community cloud. The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organizations that have shared concerns (e.g., mission, security requirements, policy, and compliance considerations).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: Which cloud deployment model is provisioned for open use by the general public?
notes.back: Public cloud.
notes.explanation: Unlike the other models, SP 800-145 says it exists on the premises of the cloud provider.
notes.evidence: Public cloud. The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for open use by the general public. It may be owned, managed, and operated by a business, academic, or government organization, or some combination of them. It exists on the premises of the cloud provider.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: Which cloud deployment model combines two or more distinct cloud infrastructures that stay unique but are bound together for data and application portability?
notes.back: Hybrid cloud.
notes.explanation: SP 800-145 gives cloud bursting for load balancing between clouds as an example.
notes.evidence: Hybrid cloud. The cloud infrastructure is a composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures (private, community, or public) that remain unique entities, but are bound together by standardized or proprietary technology that enables data and application portability (e.g., cloud bursting for load balancing between clouds).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: Five regional hospitals with the same regulatory duties commission a cloud for their use alone, run by a third party. Which deployment model is this?
notes.back: Community cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Community cloud
B) Public cloud
C) Private cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B: a public cloud is open to the general public. C: a private cloud serves a single organisation, not several.
notes.explanation: A community cloud serves consumers from several organisations with shared concerns such as compliance, and a third party may run it.
notes.evidence: The cloud infrastructure is provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of consumers from organizations that have shared concerns (e.g., mission, security requirements, policy, and compliance considerations).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, Section 2, Deployment Models, PDF p. 7

notes.front: In NIST IR 8259r1, what does "securability" mean for an IoT product?
notes.back: The product offers product cybersecurity capabilities: features or functions from its devices and components, or related manufacturer services.
notes.explanation: IR 8259r1 counts both technical means (hardware and software) and non-technical services, such as vulnerability disclosure programmes.
notes.evidence: Securability means the IoT products offer product cybersecurity capabilities—cybersecurity features or functions that the IoT devices and other product components provide through their own technical means (i.e., hardware and software) or related non-technical services from the manufacturer (i.e., vulnerability disclosure programs).
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: In NIST IR 8259r1, what is Activity 0, the first of the pre-market activities?
notes.back: Prioritise cybersecurity and maintain cybersecurity posture.
notes.explanation: Activities 1 to 5 then run from identifying expected customers to planning adequate support for their needs and goals.
notes.evidence: Activity 0: Prioritize Cybersecurity and Maintain Cybersecurity Posture. o Activity 1: Identify Expected Customers and Define Expected Use Cases.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Section 1.2, Document Structure, PDF p. 11

notes.front: Which NIST IR 8259r1 activities apply after sale (post-market)?
notes.back: Activities 6 to 8: ongoing support through end of life, and deciding how and what to communicate to customers.
notes.explanation: IR 8259r1 separates these from Activities 0 to 5, which are pre-market.
notes.evidence: The Section 4 activities are: o Activity 6: On-Going Support of Product Cybersecurity through-out the Lifecyle and through End-of-Life. o Activity 7: Define Approaches for Communicating to Customers. o Activity 8: Decide What to Communicate to Customers and How to Communicate It.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Section 1.2, Document Structure, PDF p. 11

notes.front: A manufacturer is designing a Wi-Fi door lock with a motor. When does NIST IR 8259r1 say the product's cybersecurity must begin?
notes.back: In the product planning phase.
notes.choices:
A) In the product planning phase
B) After the first incident in the field
C) At the product's end of life
notes.choicesExplained: B: waiting for an incident misses the chance to allocate resources to threat modelling. C: end of life is part of post-market support, not the start.
notes.explanation: Planning is when decision-makers can allocate resources to modelling and prioritising threats.
notes.evidence: Cybersecurity of an IoT product must begin in the product planning phase when the decision-makers are able to allocate resources towards modeling and prioritizing threats
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: What does SP 800-204 say the presence of multiple microservices does to an application's attack surface?
notes.back: It exposes a large attack surface.
notes.explanation: Every transaction also involves sending messages across a network, so network security, reliability and latency become critical.
notes.evidence: Network security, reliability, and latency are critical factors since every transaction implemented using this type of system will involve the transmission of messages across a network. Further, the presence of multiple microservices exposes a large attack surface.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-204, Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: A retailer splits its application into 40 microservices but wants its mobile app to call one address for all requests. What should it deploy?
notes.back: An API gateway.
notes.choices:
A) An API gateway
B) A type 1 hypervisor
C) A programmable logic controller
notes.choicesExplained: B: a hypervisor manages guest operating systems, not client requests. C: a PLC controls industrial processes.
notes.explanation: An API gateway provides a single entry point for all clients to the application's many microservices.
notes.evidence: Hence, it makes sense to provide a single entry point for all clients to multiple component microservices of the application.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-204, Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems, Section 2.3, API Gateway, PDF p. 17

notes.front: Which container component carries the risk that, being a static archive, it may be missing critical security updates?
notes.back: The image.
notes.explanation: An image built fully up to date can still acquire known vulnerabilities as time passes.
notes.evidence: Because images are effectively static archive files that include all the components used to run a given app, components within an image may be missing critical security updates or are otherwise outdated.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 3.1.1, Image vulnerabilities, PDF p. 25

notes.front: A team pulls images, which contain proprietary code and embedded secrets, from its image store over an unencrypted connection. Which SP 800-190 risk area is this?
notes.back: Registry risk: insecure connections to registries.
notes.choices:
A) Registry risk: insecure connections to registries
B) Orchestrator risk: unbounded administrative access
C) Host operating system risk: shared kernel
notes.choicesExplained: B: that risk concerns orchestrator users with environment-wide control. C: that risk concerns the attack surface of a shared kernel.
notes.explanation: Over insecure channels, image contents face the same confidentiality risks as any other data in transit.
notes.evidence: Images often contain sensitive components like an organization’s proprietary software and embedded secrets. If connections to registries are performed over insecure channels, the contents of images are subject to the same confidentiality risks as any other data transmitted
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 3.2.1, Insecure connections to registries, PDF p. 26

notes.front: Which container component was historically designed on the assumption that every user is an administrator with environment-wide control?
notes.back: The orchestrator.
notes.explanation: SP 800-190 files this under unbounded administrative access, since one orchestrator may run many apps managed by different teams.
notes.evidence: Historically, many orchestrators were designed with the assumption that all users interacting with them would be administrators and those administrators should have environment-wide control.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 3.3.1, Unbounded administrative access, PDF p. 27

notes.front: Which container risk arises because, by default in most runtimes, containers can reach each other and the host operating system over the network?
notes.back: Unbounded network access from containers.
notes.explanation: A compromised container could use that access to expose other resources in the environment to risk.
notes.evidence: By default in most container runtimes, individual containers are able to access each other and the host OS over the network. If a container is compromised and acting maliciously, allowing this network traffic may expose other resources in the environment to risk.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 3.4.2, Unbounded network access from containers, PDF p. 28

notes.front: Which host operating system risk in SP 800-190 gives a larger inter-object attack surface than is seen with hypervisors?
notes.back: The shared kernel.
notes.explanation: This holds even for container-specific operating systems, which otherwise have a much smaller attack surface.
notes.evidence: the use of a shared kernel invariably results in a larger inter-object attack surface than seen with hypervisors, even for container-specific OSs.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 3.5.2, Shared kernel, PDF p. 30

notes.front: Container runtimes versus hypervisors: which provides the higher level of isolation, per SP 800-190?
notes.back: Hypervisors. Containers share a kernel, so container runtime isolation is not as high.
notes.explanation: SP 800-190 grants that containers give strong software-level isolation, yet the shared kernel still widens the attack surface.
notes.evidence: although containers provide strong software-level isolation of resources, the use of a shared kernel invariably results in a larger inter-object attack surface than seen with hypervisors, even for container-specific OSs. In other words, the level of isolation provided by container runtimes is not as high as that provided by hypervisors.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 3.5.2, Shared kernel, PDF p. 30

notes.front: In SP 800-215, where does much of the computing take place in edge computing?
notes.back: Close to the location of multiple IoT devices, which may be geographically dispersed.
notes.explanation: SP 800-215 lists edge computing among the features of the current enterprise network landscape.
notes.evidence: Edge computing [1], where much of the computing takes place close to the location of multiple IoT devices that may be geographically dispersed
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, Section 2, Enterprise network landscape, PDF p. 14

notes.front: What can a hypervisor do with a host's resources to keep guest operating systems apart?
notes.back: Partition the resources and isolate each guest so it reaches only its own, plus possibly shared resources such as host files.
notes.explanation: SP 800-125 adds that each guest operating system can be fully encapsulated, which makes it portable.
notes.evidence: The hypervisor can partition the system’s resources and isolate the guest OSs so that each has access to only its own resources, as well as possible access to shared resources such as files on the host OS. Also, each guest OS can be completely encapsulated, making it portable.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What are two negative security implications of full virtualisation given in SP 800-125?
notes.back: Any two: extra layers raise the management burden; one compromise has a larger impact; easy sharing between systems can become an attack vector.
notes.explanation: Each follows from adding a layer and placing many systems on a single physical computer.
notes.evidence: Virtualization adds layers of technology, which can increase the security management burden by necessitating additional security controls. Also, combining many systems onto a single physical computer can cause a larger impact if a security compromise occurs. Further, some virtualization systems make it easy to share information between the systems; this convenience can turn out to be an attack vector
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: Why does SP 800-125 say even bare-metal hypervisors need physical security?
notes.back: Someone who can reboot the host computer might be able to alter some of the hypervisor's security settings.
notes.explanation: Hosted hypervisors are exposed differently: their management software can be used by anyone at the keyboard and mouse.
notes.evidence: hosted hypervisors are typically controlled by management software that can be used by anyone with access to the keyboard and mouse. Even bare metal hypervisors require physical security: someone who can reboot the host computer that the hypervisor is running on might be able to alter some of the security settings for the hypervisor.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies, Executive Summary, PDF p. 7

notes.front: Bare-metal (type 1) versus hosted (commonly type 2) virtualisation: where does the hypervisor run in each?
notes.back: Bare metal: directly on the hardware, with no host operating system. Hosted: on top of a host operating system such as Windows, Linux or macOS.
notes.explanation: SP 800-125 uses the terms "bare metal" and "hosted"; the type 1 and type 2 labels are common usage, not SP 800-125's.
notes.evidence: In the other form of full virtualization, known as hosted virtualization, the hypervisor runs on top of the host OS; the host OS can be almost any common operating system such as Windows, Linux, or MacOS.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies, Section 2, Full Virtualization Overview, PDF p. 11

notes.front: A data centre wants to run many server virtual machines with no general-purpose operating system underneath the hypervisor. Which architecture fits?
notes.back: A bare-metal (type 1) hypervisor.
notes.choices:
A) A bare-metal (type 1) hypervisor
B) A hosted hypervisor
C) A container runtime
notes.choicesExplained: B: a hosted hypervisor runs on top of a host operating system. C: containers share one operating system kernel instead of running full virtual machines.
notes.explanation: SP 800-125 says servers are most often virtualised with bare-metal virtualisation.
notes.evidence: Servers are most often virtualized on computers using bare metal virtualization. Desktops are most often virtualized on computers with hosted virtualization.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125, Guide to Security for Full Virtualization Technologies, Section 2, Full Virtualization Overview, PDF p. 12
